title: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, 1998
text:
INTRODUCTORY NOTE

The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court was
        		  adopted on 17 July 1998 at the conclusion of the United Nations Diplomatic
        		  Conference of Plenipotentiaries on the Establishment of the International
        		  Criminal Court (ICC or Court), held in Rome from 15 to 17 July 1998. It entered
        		  into force on 1 July 2002 upon the deposit of its 60
th
instrument of
        		  ratification, and it has 125 States Parties as of the time of writing.
The adoption of the Rome Statute marked the culmination of
                  a long-standing aspiration of the international community towards the
                  establishment of a permanent international criminal tribunal with jurisdiction over
                  âthe most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a wholeâ
                  (Rome Statute, Preamble).
The political and diplomatic process leading to this momentous
                  result was complex and spanned over fifty years. After the unsuccessful efforts
                  to establish criminal accountability at the end of the First World War, it was
                  in the wake of the Second World Warâs atrocities that international criminal
                  justice saw its foundational period, with the establishment of the two
                  International Military Tribunals in Nuremberg and Tokyo. In 1948, shortly after
                  the closure of the two tribunals, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) requested
                  the International Law Commission (ILC) to prepare a draft statute for the
                  establishment of a permanent international criminal court. Two drafts were
                  adopted in 1951 and 1953. However, the political contrapositions of the Cold
                  War prevented the project from developing further, leading to decades of
                  stalemate.
Only at the end of the Cold War and amidst the horrific conflicts
                  in the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, unveiling the commission of large-scale
                  atrocities, the international community was able to revitalize the project of
                  international criminal justice, establishing â by means of UN Security Council
                  Resolutions adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter â the two
ad hoc
International
                  Criminal Tribunals in 1993 and 1994.
In this renewed climate of international cooperation, the
                  General Assembly requested the ILC to prepare a new draft statute for a
                  permanent international criminal court, which was adopted and submitted to the
                  General Assembly in 1994. The decision was then made to establish an
Ad Hoc
Committee, which convened in April and August 1995 to consider the issues
                  arising out of the draft statute and the arrangements for convening a
                  diplomatic conference. The General Assembly later established the Preparatory
                  Committee, with the task of preparing the consolidated text of a convention on
                  the establishment of the international criminal court to serve as the basis for
                  negotiations. After multiple meetings held between 1996, 1997, and 1998 the
                  draft convention was submitted to the Conference.
The representatives of 160 States participated in the
                  Conference, along with numerous intergovernmental and non-governmental
                  organizations, specialized UN agencies, programs, and bodies. After intense negotiations,
                  a political compromise was reached on key legal and institutional aspects â
                  among which the definition of the crimes, the Courtâs jurisdiction and triggering
                  procedures, its relationship with the United Nations, and the cooperation
                  regime â and the Final Act of the Conference containing the text of the Statute
                  was adopted with 120 votes in favor, 7 votes against, and 21 abstentions. The
                  Rome Statute was opened for signature on the day of
adoption,
                    and
later deposited with the Secretary General of the United Nations.
The Rome Statute consists of a solemn Preamble and 128 articles,
                  organized in twelve Parts. It is significantly longer and more detailed compared
                  to the Statutes of the
ad hoc
tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and
                  Rwanda. Although the Statute does not create a completely self-contained legal
                  regime, it provides a consolidation and, in some respects, a more comprehensive
                  codification of key aspects of both substantive and procedural international
                  criminal law.
The Preamble of the Statute recognizes that the commission
                  of international crimes endangers international peace and security and proclaims
                  that âthe most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a
                  whole must not go unpunishedâ. Putting an end to impunity is considered
                  paramount âto contribute to the prevention of such crimesâ. The Preamble emphasizes
                  a structural feature of the Court, known as the principle of complementarity.
                  This principle entails that it is first and foremost the duty of States to
                  investigate and prosecute international crimes at the domestic level. Contrary
                  to the
ad hoc
tribunals, which enjoyed primacy over national
                  jurisdictions, the Courtâs role is complementary to national
jurisdictions
and its involvement is confined to instances in which States are either
                  unwilling or unable to genuinely investigate and prosecute alleged
                  international crimes. This principle is operationalized through the
                  admissibility regime provided under Articles 17, 18, and 19 of the Statute.
Article 5 of the Rome Statute defines the Courtâs
                  jurisdiction
ratione
materiae
, which extends to
                  the core crimes of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and
                  aggression. The crime of aggression was included since the beginning in the
                  list of crimes under the jurisdiction of the Court, but due to the lack of
                  agreement among States its legal definition and jurisdictional regime were only
                  agreed upon at the Kampala Review Conference, where the aggression amendments were
                  adopted (Resolution RC/Res.6 of 11 June 2010). In addition to core crimes, pursuant
                  to Article 70, the Court has jurisdiction on offences against the
                  administration of justice, such as the falsification of testimony or evidence;
                  impeding, corrupting, or retaliating against witness or officials of the Court;
                  or otherwise interfering with the evidence gathering process.
While the definition of the crime of genocide contained in
                  Article 6 of the Statute reproduces
verbatim
that of Article II of the
                  1948 Convention on the Prevention and Repression of the Crime of Genocide,
                  Article 7 on crimes against humanity and Article 8 on war crimes constitute an
                  important consolidation and development of substantive international criminal
                  law.
Article 7 (âCrimes against humanityâ) provides the most
                  comprehensive and up-to-date list of acts that may constitute such crimes,
                  which unlike other international crimes have yet to be codified in a dedicated
                  international convention. The provision establishes the contextual element for
                  the listed acts, which must be committed âas part of a widespread and
                  systematic attack directed against any civilian population, with knowledge of
                  the attackâ. Moreover, paragraph 2(a) of the provision specifies that, for the
                  purposes of the Statute, an attack âmeans a course of action involving the
                  multiple commission of [such acts], pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or
                  organizational policy to commit such crimesâ.
Article 7 gives special attention to crimes that have been
                  under-prosecuted at the international level until the advent of the
ad hoc
tribunals, such as sexual and
                  gender-based crimes. Article 7(1)(g) lists as separate offences ârape, sexual
                  slavery, enforced prostitution, forced pregnancy, enforced sterilization, or
                  any other form of sexual violence of comparable gravityâ. The case law of the
                  Court interpreted the residual category of âother inhumane actsâ under Article
                  7(1)(k) to comprise other gendered crimes, such as forced marriage (
Prosecutor
                    v.
Ongwen
, ICC-02/04-01/15-1762-Red, paras.
                  2741-2753). Article 7(1)(
i
) of the Statute explicitly
                  criminalizes enforced disappearance for the first time in the statute of an
                  international criminal tribunal. Article 7(1)(j) extends the Courtâs
                  jurisdiction to the crime of apartheid, which had been defined for the first
                  time in the 1973 International Convention on the Suppression and Punishment of
                  the Crime of Apartheid.
Article 8 (âWar crimesâ) is one of the most complex
                  provisions of the Rome Statute. This article provides the most comprehensive
                  list of acts that violate rules of international humanitarian law and attract
                  individual criminal liability under either conventional or customary
                  international law. Despite the progressive convergence between the law of war
                  crimes in international and non-international armed conflicts, the Statute
                  maintains separate lists of prohibited acts in the two situations.
Article 8(2)(a) lists as war crimes in international armed
                  conflicts eight acts constituting âgrave breachesâ of the Geneva Conventions of
                  1949. Letter (b) of the provision lists an additional twenty-nine acts that
                  constitute âother serious violations of the law and customs applicable in
                  international armed conflictsâ. Among such acts are intentional attacks against
                  the civilian population or objects; disproportionate attacks; intentional
                  attacks against specially protected buildings, places, facilities, or
                  personnel; killing or wounding persons
hors de combat
; pillaging; using
                  prohibited weapons or methods of warfare (among which the use of human shields
                  and starvation); rape and other forms of sexual violence; and child soldiering.
                  Regarding non-international armed conflicts, Article 8(2)(c) criminalizes four
                  acts constituting serious violations of Article 3 Common to the four Geneva
                  Conventions, while letter (e) lists nineteen acts that constitute âother
                  serious violations of the laws and customs applicable in armed conflicts not of
                  an international characterâ. Some of the acts included in the two lists of
                  âother serious violationsâ were introduced by means of amendments to the
                  Statute, which are currently in force only for the States Parties that have
                  accepted them pursuant to Article 121(5). The Court gave significant
                  contributions to the interpretation of war crimes, especially
with regard to
sexual and gender-based violence and the
                  crime of enlisting, conscripting or using children below the age of fifteen to
                  participate actively in the hostilities.
Article 8
bis
(âCrime of aggressionâ) was adopted in
                  2010 at the Kampala Review Conference and defines acts of aggression by
renvoi
to UNGA Resolution 3314 (XXIX) of 14 December 1974. For the purposes of the
                  Statute, the planning, preparation, initiation or execution of such acts
                  constitute the crime of aggression when put in place âby a person in a position
                  effectively to exercise control over or to direct the political or military
                  action of a Stateâ and when the act âby its character, gravity and scale,
                  constitutes a manifest violation of the Charter of the United Nationsâ.
Articles 11 to 15 of the Statute define the jurisdiction and
                  the triggering mechanisms of the International Criminal Court. The Court only possesses
                  jurisdiction with respect to crimes committed after the entry into force of the
                  Statute. As to jurisdiction
ratione loci
, the Court, according to
                  Article 12(2), has jurisdiction over conduct put in place: a) on the territory
                  of a State Party, irrespective of the nationality of the alleged perpetrator;
                  and/or b) by a national of a State Party, irrespective of the place of
                  perpetration. The principle of universal jurisdiction, either in a pure or
                  conditional form, was proposed by some delegations in Rome but did not obtain
                  sufficient political support to be adopted.
Article 13 of the Statute lists the procedures to trigger
                  the Courtâs jurisdiction, which were the object of extensive debate at the
                  preparatory stage and at the Rome Conference. There was broad agreement among
                  delegations on two triggering mechanisms, namely the possibility that the Court
                  be activated by means of a referral by a State Party and by a referral of the
                  UN Security Council acting under Chapter VII of the Charter (Article 13(a) and
                  (b), respectively). The third mechanism, the possibility to trigger the Court through
                  a
proprio motu
of the independent Prosecutor, was among the most
                  contentious issues discussed in Rome. This possibility was strongly supported
                  by like-minded
States and opposed by some delegations, who feared that
                  this would have given the Prosecutor excessive and unchecked discretion. A
                  compromise among the different positions was reached and resulted in the
                  formulation of Article 15. According to this provision the Prosecutor can proceed
proprio motu
with an investigation in the absence of a State or UNSC
                  referral, but he or she must submit a formal request to that effect and obtain the
                  judicial authorization of a Pre-Trial Chamber (PTC), based on the âreasonable
                  basis to proceedâ evidentiary standard.
Articles 15
bis
and
ter
, also introduced at
                  the Kampala Review Conference, contain a special and significantly more
                  restrictive jurisdictional regime for the crime of aggression, which aims to
                  coordinate the respective competences of the Court and the UN Security Council regarding
                  the ascertainment of an act of aggression. The Courtâs jurisdiction on the
                  crime of aggression was activated by means of a resolution of the Assembly of
                  the States Parties, adopted by
consensus
in 2017 (ICC-ASP/16/Res.5).
                  This resolution clarified that, in the case of a
State
referral or
proprio motu
, the Court cannot exercise its jurisdiction
                  regarding a crime of aggression when committed by a national or on the
                  territory of a State Party that has not ratified or accepted the aggression
                  amendments. By explicit provision of Article 15
bis
(5) the Courtâs
                  jurisdiction is also excluded when the alleged crime of aggression is committed
                  by a national or on the territory of State that is not a party to the Statute. Due
                  to this restrictive jurisdictional regime and the limited ratification or
                  acceptance of the aggression amendments (49 State Parties as of the date of
                  writing) the Court has yet to exercise its jurisdiction on the crime of
                  aggression.
Articles 17, 18, and 19 deal with the admissibility of
                  situations and cases before the Court and the potential judicial challenges on
                  this matter. These provisions are central to the proper allocation of labor
                  between the ICC and national jurisdictions
on the basis of
the principle of complementarity. Article 17
, in particular,
                    defines
two essential requirements for (potential) cases to be
                  admissible before the Court: complementarity and sufficient gravity. Complementarity
                  revolves around the concepts of unwillingness and inability to genuinely
                  investigate and prosecute by a State Party, as defined by Article 17(2)-(3) of
                  the Statute and further elaborated in the case law of the Court. A third
                  requirement for admissibility is the absence of
ne bis in idem
, as
                  defined under Article 20. Even when the (potential or actual) case would be admissible
                  under these criteria, the Prosecutor may discretionally decide not to proceed
                  with an investigation or prosecution if there are substantial reasons to
                  believe that they would not serve the âinterests of justiceâ (Article 53(1)(c)
                  and (2)(c)). The Prosecutor considers this possibility to be exceptional and
                  has never invoked the clause to deny the opening of an investigation or
                  prosecution. Discretional decisions not to proceed with or to stop an
                  investigation or prosecution can be judicially reviewed by the PTC under
                  Article 53.
Article 21 of the Statute (âApplicable lawâ), similarly to
                  Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice, lists the
                  sources of law applicable by the Court. This article does not create a formal
                  hierarchy of applicable sources but mandates judges to apply âin the first
                  placeâ the Statute, the Elements of Crimes and the Rules of Procedure and
                  Evidence. Only âin the second placeâ, and where appropriate, should judges
                  resort to applicable treaties and rules of customary international law. General
                  principles of law derived from national legal systems have a merely residual
                  application. The Court may apply principles and rules of law as interpreted in
                  its previous decisions, but precedents are not binding. The application and
                  interpretation of these sources must be consistent with internationally
                  recognized human rights and be without adverse distinction based on the listed
                  impermissible grounds.
Part 3 of the Rome Statute (âGeneral principles of criminal
                  lawâ) contains, for the first time in the founding document of an international
                  criminal tribunal, a comprehensive list of provisions akin to those found in
                  the general part of national criminal codes and, sometimes, in national constitutions.
                  These include fundamental guarantees such as the
nullum
crimen/
nulla
poena
sine
lege
principle, which encompasses the principle of
                  strict construction of criminal law and the prohibition of analogy (Articles
                  22-23), and the principle of non-retroactivity (Article 24).
Article 25 is particularly important as it defines in
                  detail the modes of liability under the Statute. Unlike the statutes of other
                  international and internationalized tribunals, this provision is based on a
                  differentiated approach to criminal liability, which distinguishes different
                  forms of perpetration and participation in the commission of a crime, carrying
                  a different degree of blameworthiness. It also defines what constitutes a
                  punishable attempted crime. This provision is complemented by Article 27 (âIrrelevance
                  of official capacityâ), excluding the relevance of immunities, which cannot constitute
                  a bar to the exercise of the Courtâs jurisdiction, and by Article 28 on the omissive
                  form of liability known as superior or command responsibility. Article 30 on
mental element
establishes that,
                  unless otherwise provided, the material elements of the prohibited conduct must
                  be put in place âwith intent and knowledgeâ. A different mental element, more
                  demanding (such as special intent), or less demanding (such as recklessness or
                  negligence), can be stipulated by the specific incriminating provisions. Articles
                  31, 32, and 33 deal with âgrounds for excluding criminal responsibilityâ or
                  defenses, such as mental incapacitation, intoxication, self-defense, duress,
                  mistake of fact or law, and superior orders. All offences under the Statute are
                  not subject to any statute of limitations (Article 29).
Part 4 of the Statute deals with the election,
                  organization, functioning, and articulation of the Courtâs main organs, namely
                  the Chambers (including the Presidency), the Office of the Prosecutor, and the
                  Registry. The qualifications required to serve as judges do not differ
                  significantly from those stipulated for other international (criminal)
                  tribunals, except for the more specific focus on criminal law and procedure
                  experience of the candidates (Article 36(3)(a)). Article 112 of the Statute
                  regulates the powers and duties of the political governing body of the Court,
                  the Assembly of States Parties (ASP). These include the election of Judges,
                  Prosecutor and Deputy-Prosecutors, oversight on the overall management of the
                  Court, financial and budgetary decisions, and oversight on cases of
                  non-cooperation.
Part 5 of the Statute concerns the fundamentals of criminal
                  procedure and the articulation of the various phases of investigations and
                  trials before the Court. These are further elaborated by the Rules of Procedure
                  and Evidence and the Regulations of the Court. The model of criminal procedure adopted
                  by the Statute is the result of an original merging and juxtaposition of elements
                  from different legal traditions (adversarial and inquisitorial). The most
                  evident departure from the model of
ad hoc
tribunals concerns the role
                  of the Pre-Trial Chamber, whose power and functions are defined in Article 57.
                  This section of the Court
is in charge of
important functions
                  in the preservation of evidence ahead of trial, protection of victims and, most
                  importantly, filtering and judicial review of prosecutorial decisions. These
                  powers include authorizing the Prosecutor to proceed
proprio motu
;
                  issuing arrest warrants and summonses to appear (and requesting State
                  cooperation to enforce them); reviewing other discretionary decisions of the
                  Prosecutor; and deciding on the confirmation of the charges. Through its
                  decision on the confirmation of charges the PTC checks whether there is
                  âsufficient evidence to establish substantial grounds to believeâ that the
                  accused committed the alleged crimes and decides on what charges and for what
                  modes of liability to commit him or her to trial. Trials can only be held in
                  the presence of the accused person (Article 63), who is presumed innocent until
                  proven guilty beyond reasonable doubts (Article 66).
Another important innovation of the Statute concerns the
                  role of victims in the proceedings before the ICC. Unlike at other
                  international criminal tribunals, victims are allowed to participate âat stages
                  of the proceedings determined to be appropriate by the Courtâ,
in order to
present their âviews and concernsâ (Article 68).
                  The victimsâ contribution to the establishment of the truth has acquired
                  increasing importance in the judicial practice of the Court. Victims, through
                  their legal representatives and the activity of the Office of the Public
                  Counsel have become an important procedural actor, despite not being formally a
                  party to pre-trial, trial, and appellate proceedings. The Court must ensure
                  their safety and well-being, taking the necessary measures of protection. Furthermore,
                  Article 75 establishes that victims are entitled to seek and obtain reparation for
                  the prejudice suffered
as a consequence of
the crimes.
                  The Court has adopted important decisions on the principles applicable to
                  reparations (
Prosecutor v. Lubanga
, ICC-01/04-01/06-2904) and several
                  reparation orders in cases where a conviction was entered (
Prosecutor v. Lubanga
, ICC-01/04-01/06-3129-AnxA,
Prosecutor v. Katanga
,
                  ICC-01/04-01/07-3728-tENG;
Prosecutor v.
                    Ntaganda
, ICC-01/04-02/06-2659;
Prosecutor
                      v.
Ongwen
, ICC-02/04-01/15-2074;
Prosecutor v. Al Mahdi
,
                  ICC-01/12-01/15-236). The execution of reparation orders can be made in whole
                  or in part through the Trust Fund for Victims created under Article 79. There
                  is a growing trend favoring collective reparations, frequently in the form of
                  rehabilitation
programmes
to the benefit of victims.
Decisions on criminal liability and sentences can be
                  adopted unanimously or by majority and can be issued jointly or separately. Sentencing
                  and applicable penalties (imprisonment and fines) are governed by Articles 76,
                  77, and 78 of the Statute, which are further integrated by the relevant Rules of
                  Procedure and Evidence (such as Rule 145 on aggravating and mitigating
                  factors). The Statute does not establish a precise sentencing range for each
                  crime or category of crimes. As to imprisonment, the Court may impose it for a
                  specified number of years, not exceeding a maximum of 30 years. Life-imprisonment
                  can only be imposed when justified by the extreme gravity of the offence and
                  the individual circumstances of the convicted person. Decisions on criminal
                  liability and sentences can be appealed on the specific grounds provided for
                  under Article 81 of the Statute.
Parts 9 and 10 of the Statute concern issues of
                  cooperation, judicial assistance, and enforcement of judgments. The
                  International Criminal Court relies entirely on the willingness of States
                  Parties to cooperate and provide the necessary assistance in the execution and
                  enforcement of all its major decisions. Nevertheless, drafters created a
                  quasi-vertical cooperation regime, in which States Parties must ensure full
                  cooperation with the Court and are not permitted, except on very limited
                  grounds, to postpone or deny the execution of the Courtâs requests for
                  cooperation. This is particularly true for the obligation to fulfil a request
                  of arrest and surrender of persons sought by the Court (Article 89). Article 93
                  deals with âOther forms of cooperationâ, such as the taking of evidence, the
                  provision of documents, and searches and seizures. The Prosecutor concluded in
                  2004 a cooperation agreement with INTERPOL to enhance its operational
                  capabilities and get assistance from that organization and national police
                  forces with its investigations and prosecutions.
Unfortunately, there have been in practice several violations
                  of the obligation to cooperate, especially in the arrest and surrender of
                  suspects. In these cases, States invoked alleged obstacles to cooperation,
                  mostly relating to immunities under Article 98 or competing requests by other
                  States under Article 90. Under Article 87(7) of the Statute, the Court can
                  ascertain the Stateâs international responsibility for failure to fulfil its
                  obligation to cooperate and may decide to defer the situation to the Assembly of
                  the States Parties and to the UN Security Council, if the situation was
                  referred to the Court by that body. In its case law, the Court established that
                  personal immunities such as those owed under treaty or customary international
                  law to sitting Heads of State or Government (including those of non-State
                  Parties), are ânot opposable in proceedings before the Courtâ. Hence, States
                  Parties and States that have accepted the Courtâs jurisdiction under Article
                  12(3) cannot invoke immunities as a justification not to fulfil a request of
                  cooperation for arrest and surrender (
Prosecutor
                    v. Al-Bashir
, ICC-02/05-01/09-397-Corr, paras 5, 130-132;
Situation in Ukraine
, ICC-01/22-90, paras
                  35-36).
The Rome Statute does not permit States to make
                  reservations (Article 120). A complex amendment procedure, which requires a
                  qualified majority in the Assembly of States Parties for approval is provided under
                  Article 121. Amendments to Articles 5, 6, 7, and 8 can enter into force separately
                  with respect to the accepting States Parties, one year after the deposit of the
                  instrument of acceptance. Amendments to the Statute have also been adopted in
                  the context of the special review procedure envisaged under Article 123, that
                  was the case in 2010 in Kampala.
To date, all the substantive amendments except those
                  relating to the crime of aggression, have been adopted in respect of Article 8
                  of the Statute to the effect of adding additional prohibited acts to the lists
                  of âother serious violations of laws and customs of warâ applicable in
                  international and non-international armed conflicts. In particular, the
                  amendments concerned the use of certain kinds of weapons, for instance, extending
                  the prohibition of poisonous and asphyxiating weapons, as well as of expanding
                  and flattening bullets, to non-international armed conflicts; prohibiting the
                  use of microbial and biological weapons; prohibiting weapons the primary effect
                  of which is to injure by fragments which escape detection by X-rays; and
                  prohibiting laser weapons designed to cause permanent blindness in both categories
                  of conflict. The most recent amendment, adopted at the 18
th
annual session
                  of the ASP in 2019, extends to non-international armed conflicts the
                  prohibition on the use of starvation as a method of warfare. At the 14
th
annual session of the ASP held in 2015, an amendment was adopted to delete
                  Article 124, a much-criticized transitional provision which allowed a State,
                  upon becoming party to the Statute, to exclude the Courtâs jurisdiction in
                  respect of war crimes allegedly committed by its nationals or on its territory
                  for a period of seven years. This amendment is not yet in force because States
                  Parties have subjected it to the application of Article 121(4), requiring
                  acceptance by seven-eighths of the parties. In general, the number of States
                  that have ratified or accepted the amendments is significantly lower than the
                  number of States Parties to Statute.
States Parties can withdraw from the Rome Statute following
                  the procedure contained in Article 127, an occurrence that has taken place on a
                  few occasions since its entry into force. This provision establishes that
                  withdrawal takes effect only one year after the receipt by the depositary of a
                  written notification to this effect. During this period, a withdrawing State
                  can revoke the declaration. As of end of December 2025 two States have
                  effectively withdrawn from the Statute (Burundi and The Philippines), two have
                  revoked their withdrawal, remaining States Parties (South Africa and The
                  Gambia), and one has made a withdrawal that is yet to take effect (Hungary).
                  Other three States Parties (Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger) have announced their intention
                  to withdraw but are yet to make the required notification to the depositary. Importantly,
                  Article 127(2) establishes that withdrawal does not relieve the State from the obligations
                  (including cooperation and financial obligations) arising from the Statute
                  while it was still a Party, nor does it prejudice the powers of the Court
with regard to
any matter already under consideration prior
                  to the date on which withdrawal becomes effective.
The Rome Statute, despite its limitations, represents a
                  monumental legal and institutional effort to establish a forward-looking,
                  independent, permanent system of international criminal justice. The provisions
                  of the Statute and the decisions of the Court have exercised a significant influence
                  on the development of substantive and procedural international criminal law, with
                  significant effects both at the international and at the domestic level.
The Statute influenced the drafting of the founding
                  instruments of other international(
ized
) and
                  regionalized criminal institutions, such as the Special Court for Sierra Leone,
                  the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, the Special Tribunal for
                  Lebanon and, more recently, the Extraordinary African Chambers, the Kosovo
                  Specialist Chambers and Specialist Prosecutorâs Office, and the Special
                  Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine.
A significant number of States Parties, following the ratification
                  of the Statute, have introduced new legislation or amended existing
                  legislation,
in particular
their criminal codes
                  (including military codes) and codes of criminal procedure,
in
                    order to
bring national law in conformity with the Statute. This is
                  particularly the case for cooperation and judicial assistance, given the clear
                  obligation to cooperate fully with the Court and to ensure the availability of
                  adequate national procedures, imposed by Articles 86 and 88 of the Statute. Moreover,
                  in recent years, many States, consistent with the principle of complementarity,
                  have strengthened their capacity to investigate and prosecute international
                  crimes at the domestic level, leading to important judicial developments in the
                  interpretation and application of international criminal law.
At a historical juncture when the international legal order
                  and its institutions are facing major challenges, the Rome Statute and the
                  judicial practice of the International Criminal Court, despite their weaknesses
                  and the non-cooperating stance of certain States, continue to play a
                  fundamental role in the global discourse on crucial issues of contemporary
                  international law and to ensure the possibility of establishing accountability
                  for the gravest international crimes.
This Introductory Note was written in December 2025.
